analysis.one_liner: Makes the IRS free online tax filing program a permanent, legal part of tax law.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the IRS's free Direct File program permanent, backed by 126 House Democrats, has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since the day it was introduced with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes the IRS Direct File program — which lets people file their federal taxes online for free — into law so it cannot be quietly ended by a future administration. It forbids the Treasury Department from signing any agreement promising not to offer its own filing services, and voids any such agreements already on the books. It also requires the program to import wage data from IRS records, work on phones, offer customer support, carry no fees, and to expand until at least half of taxpayers in participating states can use it, with grants to states that integrate their own tax filing.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of taxpayers who currently pay for commercial tax software or a preparer, or who struggle through paper forms, would get a free, government-run filing option that imports their wage data automatically. Workers with simple returns, low-income filers, and people in states without income tax or whose states opt in to integrated filing benefit most. The bill specifically requires the IRS to market the program and offer live help, which tends to reach people who currently miss out on free filing options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Millions of taxpayers who pay to file

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Treasury Secretary to run a permanent, federally owned online program where taxpayers can prepare and file returns for free, with no fees allowed [S2].

Requires the program to pull data directly from IRS records to pre-fill returns, use plain language in multiple languages, work on mobile devices, offer live chat support, and be promoted through mass marketing [S2].
Prohibits any future agreement restricting the government from providing tax preparation or filing services, and voids existing agreements of that kind within 30 days [S2].

Requires eligibility to reach at least half of taxpayers in participating states starting after 2027, and directs the Secretary to keep expanding it; states that integrate their own filing get $1 million grants [S2].
Moves the deadline for employer and bank information returns to March 31, giving the IRS more time to pre-fill accurate data before filing season [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies would lose customers to a free government alternative. The Treasury and IRS would bear the cost of building, marketing, and running the program, funded by an open-ended authorization of appropriations through 2035. The bill also bars fees, so taxpayers would pay nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax-prep companies and the IRS budget

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by an unlimited authorization of appropriations, so its actual cost to taxpayers would depend on future Congresses approving the money [S2].
Eligibility is limited to participating states — those with no income tax or those that opt in and integrate state filing — so taxpayers in states that do not participate would be left out [S2].

Commercial software companies argue a government filing system competes with private products and could displace free options the industry already offers, and that a government-run system has no independent incentive to keep improving [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to taxpayers is concrete and direct: a free way to file that the bill locks in permanently and requires the government to actively promote and improve. The main costs are the public expense of running the program and lost revenue for the tax-prep industry. The design is reasonable — it bars fees, requires annual reports to Congress on usage and satisfaction, and gradually expands eligibility — though its state-by-state eligibility limit and reliance on future appropriations are real limits on how far the benefit reaches.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the same day, and the committee has taken no further action on it; with the current Congress still in session, it is waiting with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the Direct File Act of 2026 on March 4, 2026, to write the IRS Direct File program into federal law [S1].
The bill attracted 126 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors [S3].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and that is the only action recorded since [S4].

The bill text prohibits Treasury agreements that restrict government tax preparation and filing services, voids any existing ones, and establishes a permanent free online filing program under new Internal Revenue Code section 7531 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the tax preparation industry and the current committee leadership are better off: the bill has not moved, so the paid filing market stays intact and the free government alternative remains un-protected by law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax-prep companies; the bill has not advanced

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the IRS Direct File program and bar agreements restricting government filing services [S1].

for.name: 126 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic caucus, with no Republican support recorded [S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and have taken no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].

against.name: Commercial tax preparation industry
against.role: Paid tax software and preparation companies (e.g., Intuit, H&R Block)
against.what_they_did: Have long lobbied against IRS-run free filing; the bill directly targets the kind of agreements they historically secured that restrict government filing services, and would void them [S2].

sides.party_line_note: All 126 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat, with no Republican cosponsors recorded; the bill sits in a committee led by Republicans [S3, S4].

industries.industry: Commercial tax preparation and software companies
industries.note: A free, permanent, government-run filing option would directly take customers from paid software and preparers. The bill voids the kind of agreements this industry has historically used to keep the government out of filing, making their interest run against the free public option taxpayers would get [S2].

industries.industry: State tax agencies in participating states
industries.note: States that integrate their filing with the federal program would receive $1 million grants, and their residents could file state and federal returns together. This lowers filing friction for those states' residents [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no recorded committee action, and a majority the bill does not yet have in either chamber, the most likely path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress unless it is attached to a larger tax bill or the committee schedules action. Codification of Direct File would more plausibly move as part of broad tax legislation than on its own.
